contentBlocks.text: Last week you explored atomic structure. This week: chemical bonding, why atoms actually connect to each other!

Atoms bond because most elements are more stable with a full outer shell of 8 valence electrons (the octet rule), connecting directly to last week's valence-electron content. An atom with only 1 or 2 valence electrons, or one that's missing just 1 or 2 from a full shell, tends to bond in a way that achieves that stable full-shell arrangement. Using last week's periodic table knowledge, explain why sodium (1 valence electron) and chlorine (7 valence electrons) might be especially likely to bond with each other.
You just learned why atoms bond in the first place! Tomorrow we'll learn about ionic bonding specifically.

objectives: State the octet rule: atoms tend toward a stable full outer shell of 8 valence electrons
Explain why sodium and chlorine's valence-electron counts make them likely to bond
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review last week's valence-electron and periodic-table work briefly.
2. Introduce the octet rule.
3. Have the child explain why sodium and chlorine are likely to bond.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's ionic-bonding lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: point out that sodium's 1 electron and chlorine's missing 1 electron (from 8) fit together like a puzzle piece before asking for the full explanation
Ready for more: ask the child to predict whether two chlorine atoms could bond with each other in a similar way, and why or why not

teacherGuide.answerKey: Sodium has just 1 valence electron (one more than a stable, empty-outer-shell-below arrangement) and chlorine is missing just 1 electron from a full octet — sodium can give away its 1 electron and chlorine can accept it, so both atoms end up more stable, making them especially likely to bond together.
